translated_text:
Thus, in these general matters, no judge, whoever he may be—even if he is one of the Companions—may impose his own opinion by judicial ruling upon someone who disagrees with him, saying: “I have obliged him neither to act nor to issue fatwas except according to the view that accords with my school.” Rather, judgment in these questions belongs to Allah and His Messenger. The judge is but one of the Muslims: if he possesses knowledge, he should present it; and if his opponent possesses knowledge, he too should present it. If the truth becomes clear and the ruling of Allah and His Messenger is known, everyone must follow that ruling. If it remains unclear, each is allowed to retain his position—the proponent of one view retaining his position, and the proponent of the other retaining his. Neither may seek to stop the other except through knowledge, proof, and explanation, presenting whatever knowledge he possesses.

As for “physical force and coercion,” he may issue a binding ruling only in a particular case brought before him. For example, someone dies and his heirs dispute the division of his estate: if they bring their dispute before him, he divides it among them. If he rules according to one of the two scholarly opinions, he binds the litigant to his judgment. The litigant is not entitled to say: “I will not accept this unless he rules according to the other opinion.”

Likewise, if two people bring before him a dispute concerning a claim made by one against the other, he adjudicates between them as Allah and His Messenger have commanded, and obliges the party against whom judgment is given to comply with his ruling. That party is not entitled to say: “You have ruled against me according to an opinion I do not accept.” For the judge must exercise independent judgment, as the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

“When a judge exercises independent judgment and reaches the correct conclusion, he has two rewards; and when he exercises independent judgment and errs, he has one reward.”

Allah may single out certain prophets and scholars

and judges with knowledge not granted to others, as the Most High says:

“And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field in which some people’s sheep had grazed by night; We were witness to their judgment.”

“We gave Solomon understanding of the case, and to each We gave sound judgment and knowledge.”

Judges must judge only with justice. “Justice” is what Allah has revealed, as the Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners and, when you judge between people, to judge with justice. Excellent indeed is what Allah instructs you to do. Surely Allah is All-Hearing, All-Seeing.”

Then the Most High says:

“O you who believe, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. If you disagree over anything, refer it to Allah and the Messenger, if you believe in Allah and the Last Day. That is better and best in outcome.”

Thus Allah has made obedience to those in authority obligatory alongside obedience to the Messenger. He has also obliged the Muslim community, whenever they disagree, to refer their dispute to Allah and His Messenger—to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger. For Allah, glorified and exalted is He, is the Judge who judges between His servants, and judgment belongs to Him alone. Allah revealed the Scriptures and sent the messengers to judge between them. Whoever obeys the Messenger is among Allah’s pious allies and will enjoy happiness in this world and the Hereafter. Whoever disobeys the Messenger is among those destined for misery and punishment.

The Most High says:

“Mankind was one community. Then Allah sent the prophets as bearers of good tidings and warners, and sent down with them the Scripture in truth to judge between people concerning their disagreements. None differed over it except those who had been given it, after clear proofs had come to them, out of envy

among themselves. Then Allah guided those who believed, by His permission, to the truth concerning which they differed. And Allah guides whom He wills to a straight path.”

In Sahīh Muslim, Ā’ishah reports that when the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, rose to pray at night, he would say:

“O Allah, Lord of Gabriel, Michael, and Isrāfīl, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen! You judge between Your servants concerning their disagreements. Guide me, by Your permission, to the truth concerning which I differ; indeed, You guide whom You will to a straight path.”

The Most High says:

“Those who were given the Scripture did not differ until knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves.”

Thus He, glorified and exalted is He, makes clear that He guided them and made the truth clear to them. Yet some of them wrong others despite knowing the truth, following their own desires and disobeying Allah’s command. Such a person knows the truth but deviates from it, as the Most High says:

“Relate to them the story of the one to whom We gave Our signs, but who cast them off. Satan then pursued him, and he became one of those who went astray.”

“Had We willed, We would have elevated him through them, but he clung to the earth and followed his own desires. His likeness is that of a dog: if you drive it away, it pants, and if you leave it alone, it pants. Such is the likeness of those who reject Our signs. So recount these stories, that they may reflect.”

He, glorified and exalted is He, has thus made clear that He sent the messengers and sent down with them the Scripture to judge between people concerning their disagreements. The Most High says:

“Whatever you disagree about, its judgment rests with Allah. Such is Allah, my Lord; in Him I put my trust, and to Him I turn.”

Joseph said:

“O my two fellow prisoners! Are many different lords better, or Allah, the One, the All-Subduing?”

“You worship besides Him nothing but names that you and your forefathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no

authority. Judgment belongs to Allah alone. He has commanded that you worship none but Him. That is the upright religion, but most people do not know.”

Judgment thus belongs to Allah alone, and His messengers convey His message. Their judgment is His judgment, their command is His command, and obedience to them is obedience to Him. Whatever the Messenger rules, commands them to do, or prescribes as religion, all created beings must follow and obey, for that is Allah’s judgment concerning His creation.

The Messenger conveys Allah’s message. The Most High says:

“We sent no messenger except to be obeyed by Allah’s permission. If, when they wronged themselves, they had come to you and sought Allah’s forgiveness, and the Messenger had sought forgiveness for them, they would have found Allah Accepting of repentance, Merciful.”

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge concerning their disputes, then find within themselves no discomfort over what you have decided and submit fully.”

All created beings must therefore accept as their judge the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, the Seal of the Prophets, the finest of the messengers, and the most honoured of creation before Allah. No one may depart from his judgment in anything, whether a scholar, a king, a shaykh, or anyone else.

Had Moses, Jesus, or any other messenger lived to witness his coming, they would have been obliged to follow him, as the Most High says:

“And when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: ‘Whatever Scripture and wisdom I give you, should a messenger then come to you confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him.’ He said, ‘Do you affirm this and accept My binding covenant?’ They said, ‘We affirm it.’ He said, ‘Then bear witness, and I am with you among the witnesses.’”

It is reported from several of the early generations—ʿAlī, Ibn ʿAbbās, and others—that they said:

“Never

did Allah send a prophet from the time of Noah onward without taking a covenant from him that, if Muhammad were sent while he was alive, he would certainly believe in him and support him. He also commanded him to take a covenant from his people that, if Muhammad were sent while they were alive, they would certainly believe in him and support him.”

He, glorified be He, took a covenant from each earlier prophet to affirm the truth of whoever came after him, and from each later prophet to affirm the truth of whoever came before him. Thus, the prophets did not differ; rather, their religion is one, as the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in an authentic hadith:

“We prophets have one religion.”

The Most High says:

“O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds. Indeed, I know all that you do. And indeed this religion of yours is one religion, and I am your Lord, so fear Me.”

That is, your faith is one faith, as in their words:

“Indeed, we found our forefathers following a religion”—that is, a faith.

The Most High also says:

“He has ordained for you the religion He enjoined upon Noah, that which We have revealed to you, and what We enjoined upon Abraham, Moses, and Jesus: establish the religion and do not become divided over it. What you call the polytheists to is grievous to them.”

The religion of the prophets is therefore one: the religion of Islam. They were all Muslims and believers, as Allah has made clear in several places in the Quran. Some of their prescribed laws, however, differ. He may prescribe something at one time for a wise purpose, then prescribe something else at another time for a wise purpose, just as, in the early days of Islam, He prescribed

prayer facing Jerusalem. He then abrogated that ruling and commanded prayer facing the Kaaba. Thus, the prescribed law changed while the religion remained one. Facing the Levant at that time was part of the religion of Islam, as was observing the Sabbath for Moses. Once the earlier ruling was abrogated, however, the religion of Islam lay in the superseding ruling: praying towards the Kaaba. Whoever adheres to the abrogated ruling rather than the superseding one is neither following the religion of Islam nor following any of the prophets. Whoever alters the prophets’ law and invents a law of his own produces a false law that may not be followed, as Allah says:

“Or do they have partners who have ordained for them in religion what Allah has not authorized?”

This is why the Jews and Christians disbelieved: they adhered to a law that had been altered and abrogated. Allah has obliged all creation to believe in all His Books and messengers. Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is the last of the messengers, so all creation must follow him and the religion he prescribed, namely what he brought of the Book and Sunnah. What the Book and Sunnah teach is the law that all creation must follow; no one may depart from it. It is the law that those who wage jihad fight to uphold: the Book and Sunnah.

The swords of the Muslims support this law—the Book and Sunnah—as Jābir ibn ‘Abd Allāh said:

“The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, commanded us to strike with this—meaning the sword—whoever departs from this—meaning the written copy of the Quran.”

The Most High says:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance so that people may uphold justice. And We sent down

iron, in which there is great might and benefits for people, and so that Allah may know those who support Him and His messengers without seeing Him. Indeed, Allah is All-Powerful, Almighty.”

He, glorified and exalted, thus makes clear that He sent down the Book, justice, and the means by which justice is known, so that people may uphold justice; and He sent down iron. Whoever departs from the Book and the balance is fought with iron. The Book and justice are inseparable. The Book explains the prescribed law; thus, the law is justice, and justice is the law. Whoever judges justly has judged according to the law. Yet many people attribute their statements to the law when they are no part of it. They make such statements out of ignorance, error, or deliberate fabrication. This is the altered law whose proponents deserve punishment, not the revealed law that Gabriel brought from Allah to the last of the messengers. That revealed law is entirely just: it contains neither injustice nor ignorance. The Most High says:

“And if you judge, judge between them with justice. Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly.”

The Most High also says:

“And judge between them by what Allah has revealed.”

What Allah has revealed is justice, and justice is what Allah has revealed. The Most High says:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners and, when you judge between people, to judge with justice.”

The Most High also says:

“Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth so that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you.”

What Allah has shown him in His Book is justice.

Many Muslim scholars endowed with knowledge and religious devotion—from among the Companions, the Successors, and the other imams of the Muslims, such as the four imams and others—may express opinions based on their independent scholarly judgment; with regard to these opinions, it is permissible

to adopt them, and no Muslim is obliged to adhere to any statement except that of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This, then, is law involving interpretation and independent scholarly judgment. It may, in fact, accord with the revealed law, in which case the one who holds it receives two rewards; or it may not accord with it. Yet Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. If a servant fears Allah as much as he can, Allah rewards him for that and forgives his error. No one is entitled to condemn, disparage, or punish someone in this position. However, once the truth is known to contradict his opinion, it is not permissible to abandon the truth with which Allah sent His Messenger for the opinion of any created being.

That truth is the law revealed by Allah—the Quran and the Sunnah—and it is the religion of Allah and His Messenger, so that Allah’s word may be supreme and all worship may be devoted to Allah. They do not wage jihad to uphold the opinion of a scholar, a shaykh, or someone exercising interpretation. Rather, they wage jihad so that Allah alone may be worshipped and worship may be devoted to Him. Thus, it is reported in al-Musnad from Ibn ‘Umar that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“I was sent with the sword ahead of the Hour, so that Allah alone may be worshipped, without any partner. My provision has been placed beneath the shade of my spear, and humiliation and abasement have been imposed upon whoever opposes my command. Whoever imitates a people is one of them.”

The Most High says:

“Fight them until there is no more fitnah and all worship is devoted to Allah.”

In the two Sahīh collections, Abū Mūsā al-Ash‘arī reported:

“It was asked, ‘O Messenger of Allah, a man fights out of bravery, out of partisan zeal, or for show. Which of these is in Allah’s cause?’ He replied, ‘Whoever fights so that Allah’s word may be supreme is in Allah’s cause.’”

Thus, the purpose of jihad is that none should be worshipped except Allah: no one should invoke, pray to, prostrate before, or fast for anyone other than Him; perform ‘umrah or Hajj except to His House; offer sacrifices or make vows except to Him; swear except by Him; rely upon anyone but Him; fear anyone but Him; or be mindful of anyone but Him. He alone brings good and averts harm; He alone guides His creation, grants them victory, provides for them, frees them from need, and forgives their sins. The Most High says:

“Allah has said, ‘Do not take two gods. He is but One God, so fear Me alone.’

“To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, and to Him alone is worship perpetually due. Will you then fear anyone other than Allah?

“Whatever blessing you have is from Allah. Then, when hardship touches you, it is to Him that you cry for help.

“Then, when He removes the hardship from you, some of you associate partners with their Lord,

“showing ingratitude for what We have given them. So enjoy yourselves; you will soon know.”

Allah Most High has forbidden every form of associating partners with Him and setting up any rival to Him. None besides Him may be invoked—not the angels, the prophets, the righteous, the sun, the moon, the stars, idols, or anything else. Indeed, He has made clear that whoever takes the angels and prophets as lords is a disbeliever. The Most High says:

“It is not for a human being to whom Allah has given the Scripture, judgment, and prophethood to then say to people, ‘Be my servants rather than Allah’s.’ Rather, he would say, ‘Be godly scholars because of your teaching of the Scripture and your study of it.’

“Nor would he command you to take the angels and prophets as lords. Would he command you to disbelieve after you have become Muslims?”

And the Most High says:

“Say, ‘Call upon those you claim to be gods besides Him. They have no power to remove your hardship or shift it elsewhere.’

“Those whom they invoke themselves seek a means of drawing near to their Lord, seeking to be nearest to Him. They hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, your Lord’s punishment is to be feared.”

Allah, glorified and exalted is He, censures those who invoke the angels, the prophets, and other righteous people. He explains that those whom they invoke have no power to remove their hardship or shift it elsewhere. They themselves draw near to Allah through the means of approach—namely, righteous deeds—and hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. How, then, can people invoke created beings and forsake the Creator? The Most High says:

“Do those who disbelieve think they can take My servants as protectors besides Me? We have prepared Hell as a welcome for the disbelievers.”

He, glorified and exalted is He, knows His servants’ circumstances and is merciful to them, as related in an authentic hadith about the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace:

“He saw a woman among the captives who, upon seeing a child, pressed him to her belly. He said, ‘Do you think this woman would cast her child into the Fire?’ They replied, ‘No, O Messenger of Allah.’ He said, ‘Allah is more merciful to His servants than this woman is to her child.’”

He, glorified is He, is All-Hearing and Near. Allah Most High says:

“Say, ‘If I go astray, I do so only to my own detriment; but if I am guided, it is through what my Lord reveals to me. Indeed, He is All-Hearing and Near.’”

He, Most High, is Merciful and Loving. “Affection” means kindness and love. He loves His believing servants and places affection for them in people’s hearts, as the Most High says:

“Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds—the Most Merciful will grant them affection.”

Ibn ‘Abbās and others said: He loves them and makes His servants love them.

Hearing one person does not distract Him, glorified is He, from hearing another. Requests do not confuse Him, nor does He grow weary of persistent supplication. Rather, He loves those who call upon Him and implore Him, and He detests those who do not call upon Him. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah becomes angry with whoever does not ask Him.”

The Most High says:

“Your Lord says, ‘Call upon Me; I will answer you. Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me will enter Hell, humiliated.’”

And He, the Most High, exalted is He, says:

“When My servants ask you about Me, I am indeed near. I answer the supplicant’s call when he calls upon Me. So let them respond to Me and believe in Me, so that they may be rightly guided.”

Some of the Companions said, “O Messenger of Allah, is our Lord near, so that we may address Him quietly, or distant, so that we should call out to Him?” Allah then revealed this verse.

He, glorified and exalted is He, is unlike created beings, to whom requests are conveyed through barriers. Rather, in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah says, ‘I have divided the prayer into two halves between Myself and My servant: half is for Me and half is for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’ When the servant says, ‘All praise is for Allah, Lord of all worlds,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has praised Me.’ When he says, ‘The Most Merciful, the Ever-Merciful,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has extolled Me.’ When he says, ‘Master of the Day of Judgment,’ Allah says, ‘My servant has glorified Me.’

“When he says, ‘You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help,’ Allah says, ‘This verse is divided into two halves between Myself and My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’ When he says, ‘Guide us to the straight path—the path of those You have blessed, not those who have incurred Your anger, nor those who have gone astray,’ He says, ‘These verses are for My servant, and My servant shall have what he asks for.’”

He, glorified is He, will Himself speak to His servants on the Day of Resurrection, as related in the authentic collection from ʿAdī ibn Hātim, who reported that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“There is not one of you but that his Lord, mighty and majestic, will speak to him, with neither a doorkeeper nor an interpreter between them. He will look to his right and see only what he has sent ahead, and look to his left and see only what he has sent ahead. He will look before him, and the Fire will confront him. So whoever among you can protect himself from the Fire, even with half a date, should do so. If he cannot find that, then with a kind word.”

He, glorified is He, is near to those who call upon Him and draws near to those who worship and obey Him. As related in an authentic hadith, the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Allah, the Most High, says: ‘I am as My servant thinks of Me, and I am with him when he remembers Me. If he remembers Me within himself, I remember him within Myself. If he remembers Me in a gathering, I remember him in a gathering better than it. If he draws near to Me by a handspan, I draw near to him by a cubit. If he draws near to Me by a cubit, I draw near to him by an armspan. If he comes to Me walking, I come to him running.’”

Allah, glorified is He, bestows kindness, bounty and generosity upon His servants, not because He has any need of them. As the Most High says:

“And say, ‘All praise is for Allah, Who has never taken a son, nor has He any partner in His dominion, nor does He need a protector out of weakness.’ And proclaim His greatness.”

He alone calls His servants to account, and He is the One who recompenses them for their deeds:

“So whoever does an atom’s weight of good will see it, and whoever does an atom’s weight of evil will see it.”

He is the One who provides for them, grants them well-being, helps them and guides them; no one other than Him does this. The Most High says:

“Who is there to serve as an army for you, helping you against the Most Merciful? There is nothing

but delusion for the disbelievers.”

“Or who will provide for you if He withholds His provision? Yet they persist in insolence and aversion.”

The Most High also says:

“Say, ‘Who guards you by night and day from the Most Merciful?’ Yet they turn away from the remembrance of their Lord.”

The more correct of the two interpretations of this verse is that it means: Who is there to guard you in Allah’s stead? Who wards off the harms you fear from humans and jinn?

The Messenger is the intermediary and emissary between them and Allah, mighty and majestic. He conveys to them Allah’s commands and prohibitions, His promises and warnings, and what He has made lawful and forbidden. Thus, the lawful is what Allah and His Messenger have made lawful; the forbidden is what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden; and the religion is what Allah and His Messenger have prescribed. No one may depart from anything prescribed by the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is the revealed law that those in authority must require people to observe, that those engaged in jihad must fight to uphold, and that every individual must follow and support.

The revealed law binding upon all creation does not mean “a judge’s ruling,” even if the judge is the best person of his time. Rather, the ruling of a knowledgeable, just judge binds particular people who have brought a particular case before him; it does not bind all creation. Nor is any Muslim scholar obliged to follow a judge’s opinion in any matter, great or small, if he knows what Allah and His Messenger have commanded. Indeed, no individual among the general public is obliged to follow the judge’s opinion in any matter. Rather, he may seek a fatwa from anyone he is permitted to consult, even if that person is not a judge. Whenever a scholar abandons what he knows from

the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger and follows a judge’s ruling that contradicts the ruling of Allah and His Messenger, he becomes an apostate and disbeliever, deserving punishment in this world and the Hereafter. The Most High says:

“Alif Lām Mīm Sād.”

“A Book sent down to you—so let there be no distress in your heart because of it—that you may warn thereby, and as a reminder to the believers.”

“Follow what has been sent down to you from your Lord, and do not follow other protectors besides Him. How little you heed the reminder!”

Even if he were beaten, imprisoned, and subjected to all kinds of harm to make him abandon what he knows of the law of Allah and His Messenger, which he is obliged to follow, he would still deserve Allah’s punishment if he followed someone else’s ruling. Rather, he must remain patient, even if he suffers harm for Allah’s sake. This is Allah’s established way with the prophets and their followers. Allah Most High says:

“Alif Lām Mīm.”

“Do people think they will be left to say, ‘We believe,’ without being tested?”

“We certainly tested those before them. Allah will surely know those who are truthful, and He will surely know the liars.”

The Most High also says:

“We will surely test you until We know those among you who strive and those who remain steadfast, and We will put your deeds to the test.”

The Most High also says:

“Or do you think you will enter Paradise without undergoing what befell those who passed away before you? They were afflicted with hardship and suffering, and were so shaken that even the Messenger and those who believed with him said, ‘When will Allah’s help come?’ Indeed, Allah’s help is near.”

This applies when a judge has ruled on a matter open to scholarly judgment over which the Companions and Successors differed, adopting the opinion of some of them, while others know of a Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that conflicts with his ruling. Such a person must follow

what he knows of the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, enjoin it, issue fatwas in accordance with it, and call others to it, rather than defer to the judge. All of this is agreed upon by the Muslims.

If a Muslim, whether a scholar or otherwise, abandons what he knows of the command of Allah and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in favor of someone else’s opinion, he deserves punishment. The Most High says:

“So let those who oppose his command beware, lest a trial befall them or a painful punishment afflict them.”

If, however, that judge was unaware of this text—as was the case with many of the Companions, the Successors, the four imams, and others who expressed opinions on matters through independent scholarly judgment when a Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, contradicted their conclusions—then such people are excused, because they exercised independent scholarly judgment, and:

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity.”

But whoever knows the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, may not turn away from it to anything else. The Most High says:

“It is not for a believing man or woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, to have any choice in their affair. Whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has clearly gone astray.”

Whoever follows that with which Allah sent His Messenger will be guided and granted Allah’s support in this world and the Hereafter, as the Most High says:

“We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe, both in the life of this world and on the Day when the witnesses stand forth.”

The Most High also says:

“Our word has already gone forth to Our servants, the messengers:

They will surely be given victory,

And Our forces will surely prevail.”

When a calamity befalls a servant, it is because of his sin, not because he follows the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Rather, it is through following the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that

he receives mercy and support, while it is because of his sins that he is punished and forsaken. The Most High says:

“Whatever calamity befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned, and He pardons much.”

Thus, when the Muslims were defeated at Uhud, despite being with the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the enemy gained the upper hand over them, Allah explained that this was because of their sins. The Most High says:

“Those of you who turned away on the day the two armies met—it was Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned. But Allah has pardoned them. Indeed, Allah is All-Forgiving, Forbearing.”

The Most High also says:

“When a calamity befell you, although you had inflicted twice as much, did you say, ‘How has this happened?’ Say, ‘It is from yourselves.’”

He, glorified be He, explained the wisdom behind testing them. The Most High says:

“Similar situations have passed before you, so travel through the land and see how those who denied the truth met their end.”

“This is a clear explanation for mankind, and guidance and an admonition for the God-fearing.”

“Do not lose heart or grieve, for you will have the upper hand, if you are believers.”

“If you have suffered a wound, the other people have suffered a similar wound. We alternate such days among people, so that Allah may make evident those who believe and take martyrs from among you. And Allah does not love the wrongdoers.”

“And so that Allah may purify those who believe and destroy the disbelievers.”

The Most High also says:

“Whatever good befalls you is from Allah, and whatever evil befalls you is from yourself.”

Allah has decreed it, and He has decreed everything. Yet whatever well-being, victory, or provision a servant receives comes from Allah’s favor and kindness toward him. All good is from Allah; the servant has nothing of his own. Rather, he is utterly dependent and has no power

 قَالَ:

Allah has related to us in the Quran the accounts of the prophets and the harm they and their believing followers suffered for His sake. Then He granted them victory and made the final outcome theirs. He related this to us so that we might learn from it. The Most High says:

“In their stories there is certainly a lesson for people of understanding. This is not a fabricated account, but a confirmation of what came before it, an explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for people who believe.”

Thus, the divine law that every Muslim must follow, and that those in authority must uphold and wage jihad for, is the Quran and the Sunnah. Here is the foremost of judges, rulers, and kings saying: “If I award someone something he knows he is not entitled to, he must not take it.” The Muslims unanimously agree that a judge’s ruling concerning ownership as such has no effect on the underlying reality. Thus, if he awarded Zayd property belonging to ʿAmr, exercising independent legal judgment and earnestly seeking the truth, it would still not be lawful for Zayd to take it.

As for “contracts and their dissolution”—such as a ruling establishing a marriage, a divorce, a sale, or the rescission of a sale—there is a well-known disagreement. The majority hold that these rulings likewise have no effect on the underlying reality. This is a well-known issue. All this concerns a learned and just judge who has ruled on a worldly matter.

“Judges are of three kinds,” as reported in the Sunan collections from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, who said:

“Judges are of three kinds: two are in the Fire and one is in Paradise. A man who knows the truth and judges accordingly is in Paradise. A man who judges between people without knowledge is in the Fire. A man who knows the truth but rules contrary to it is in the Fire.”

Even when a judge who belongs among the people of Paradise awards someone something that the recipient knows is not rightfully his, it is unlawful for him to take it, according to the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the Muslims. What, then, if he rules on matters of religion over which he has no authority to adjudicate? In such matters, he is merely one Muslim among others: if he has knowledge, he may speak; otherwise, he must remain silent;

translated_text:
as when he rules that travel to places other than the three mosques is prescribed and recommended, that whoever undertakes it is rewarded, and that anyone who says it is not recommended is to be harmed and punished or imprisoned.

Such a ruling is invalid by the consensus of the Muslims. No one who knows the religion of Islam may follow it, nor may any ruler enforce it. Whoever enforces and supports such a ruling is subject to the same judgment as others like him: if the proof with which Allah sent His Messenger has been established against him and he contravenes it, he deserves punishment. Likewise, if he imposes such a ruling out of ignorance and obliges people to follow something of which he has no knowledge, he deserves punishment. If, however, he errs while exercising independent legal judgment, he is pardoned.

Allah has required Muslim rulers to follow the revealed law, namely the Quran and Sunnah. When Muslims disagree over a religious question, even if the person disputing it is merely an individual student of knowledge, the rulers may not compel him to follow a judge’s ruling. Rather, they must explain the truth to him, just as someone with knowledge explains the truth to someone who is ignorant. If the truth with which Allah sent His Messenger becomes clear and manifest to him, and he stubbornly opposes it thereafter, he deserves punishment.

As for someone who says, “What I have stated is my own view or the view of a group of Muslim scholars, and I have stated it on the basis of independent legal judgment or in reliance on scholarly authority,” the Muslims agree that he may not be punished, even if he has committed an error contrary to the Quran and Sunnah. Were such a person to be punished, all Muslims would be punished, for every one of them holds some mistaken views reached through independent legal judgment or reliance on scholarly authority. If Allah punished everyone who erred, He would punish all of creation. Rather, Allah Most High has said in the Quran:

“The Messenger has believed in what was sent down to him from his Lord, as have the believers. Each has believed

in Allah, His angels, His Books, and His messengers. ‘We make no distinction between any of His messengers.’ And they say, ‘We hear and obey. Grant us Your forgiveness, our Lord, and to You is the final return.’”

“Allah does not burden any soul beyond its capacity. It will have the good it has earned and bear the evil it has earned. Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake. Our Lord, do not lay upon us a burden like that which You laid upon those before us. Our Lord, do not burden us with what we cannot bear. Pardon us, forgive us, and have mercy on us. You are our Protector, so grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”

It is established in the Sahīh, on the authority of the Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace), that Allah answered this supplication. When the believers said, “Our Lord, do not hold us accountable if we forget or make a mistake,” Allah said, “I have done so.” The same applies to the rest of the supplication. The Prophet (may Allah bless him and grant him peace) also said, “Allah has pardoned my community for mistakes, forgetfulness, and what they are compelled to do.”

Thus, when a mufti, a soldier, or a layperson expresses a view according to their best judgment—whether through independent legal reasoning or reliance on scholarly authority—intending to follow the Messenger to the best of their knowledge, they do not deserve punishment, by the consensus of the Muslims, even if their error is unanimously recognized as such.

If they say, “We have spoken the truth,” and support their position with evidence from the revealed law, no judge may compel them to accept his view merely on his own authority, nor rule that his view, rather than theirs, is the truth. Rather, the Quran and Sunnah must judge between him and them. The truth with which Allah sent His Messenger must not be concealed; rather, it must be brought to light. If it becomes clear, everyone must return to it. If it does not, each side should leave the other alone. This is the case with questions disputed by adherents of the different schools of law. No one says that a follower of one school must follow someone else’s school merely because the latter is a judge, for the situation may be reversed: the other person may become a judge

translated_text:
by the Messenger, we refrain from, even if others believe it to be a means of drawing near to Allah. Our duty is to obey the Messenger, not to obey anyone who opposes him, even if that person is acting on an interpretation.”

It is well known that the People of the Book and the adherents of religious innovations engage in many forms of worship which they regard as means of drawing near to Allah and acts of obedience, although Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—has forbidden them. If someone says, “I obey the Messenger and do not engage in these forms of worship; rather, I forbid what Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—has forbidden,” how can it be permissible to oppose him? Indeed, even if he were mistaken despite exercising independent scholarly judgment, he would not deserve punishment, by the consensus of the Muslims.

Nor is he obliged to follow anyone’s ruling, by the consensus of the Muslims. A judge has no authority to rule that Allah’s Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—commanded a particular thing; that a particular deed is, or is not, an act of obedience or a means of drawing near to Allah; or that travelling to mosques and graves, including the grave of the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—is or is not prescribed. Judges have no authority in such matters beyond that shared by other Muslims. Rather, discussion of these matters is open to the entire community of Muhammad—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—and whoever possesses knowledge may speak on the basis of that knowledge.

No one has the right to pass judgment against a scholar, by the consensus of the Muslims. Rather, his error must be explained to him. If it is demonstrated to him, through scriptural evidence that must be accepted, that he has erred, and his error becomes apparent to people, yet he does not retract it but persists in publicly expressing what contradicts the Quran and the Sunnah and calling others to it, then he must be restrained from doing so and punished if he refuses to desist. But if this has not been demonstrated to him by evidence

from the revealed law, then, by the consensus of the Muslims, it is not permissible to punish him, prevent him from expressing that view, or rule that he must not express it, when he says, “This is what the Quran and Sunnah indicate, as such-and-such Muslim scholars have also stated.” If such a person exercises independent scholarly judgment and errs, he may be judged only according to the Quran and Sunnah. His opponent, however, speaks without knowledge, and the ruling he has issued has not been stated by any Muslim scholar. Even if the leading Muslim scholars expressed a view like that of the judges, they could compel people to accept it only on the basis of evidence from the revealed law, not merely on the strength of their own ruling.

For the one whom Allah has obliged people to follow and obey is the Messenger, whose judgment, command, law, and religion they must follow. He is Allah’s proof against His creation. Through him Allah distinguished between truth and falsehood, guidance and misguidance, right conduct and error, and the path to Paradise and the path to Hell. Through him Allah guided His creation. Allah Most High says:

“Indeed, We have revealed to you as We revealed to Noah and the prophets after him. And We revealed to Abraham, Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, the Tribes, Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon; and We gave David the Psalms.”

“And messengers We have already told you about, and messengers We have not told you about. And Allah spoke directly to Moses.”

“Messengers bringing good tidings and warnings, so that people would have no argument against Allah after the messengers.”

An authentic report relates that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said:

“No one loves to accept an excuse more than Allah; for that reason He sent the messengers as bearers of good tidings and warnings.”

Thus, the proof against creation is established through the messengers. What the Messenger brought is the revealed law that all people must accept, and everyone must refer their disputes to the Quran and Sunnah.

For this reason, one of the fundamental principles of the Sunnah and the community is that none of those who assumed authority after the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—such as the Rightly Guided Caliphs and others, need possess knowledge unknown to everyone else. Rather, Muslims share in knowing the religion prescribed by the Messenger—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When some possess knowledge of hadith that others do not, they convey it to them.

For this reason, the caliphs would ask the Companions concerning certain matters, “Do you have any knowledge from the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—about this?” Once the Messenger’s Sunnah became clear to them, they ruled accordingly. Thus, Abū Bakr al-Siddīq asked them about a grandmother’s inheritance when she came to him. He said, “There is no share prescribed for you in Allah’s Book, and I know of nothing prescribed for you in the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah. But let me ask the people.” He asked them, and Muhammad ibn Maslama and others informed him that the Messenger of Allah—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had awarded her one-sixth.

Likewise, “When ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb asked them about an unborn child who had been killed, one of the Companions stood and informed him that the Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—had ruled that compensation should be a male or female slave.” That is, whoever killed an unborn child was liable to give its heirs a male or female slave in compensation. So ʿUmar ruled accordingly. They stated that the slave’s value should equal one-tenth of the blood money payable for the child’s mother.

The Prophet—may Allah bless him and grant him peace—said concerning ʿUmar ibn al-Khattāb:

“Among the nations before you there were people who were inspired. If there is anyone like that in my nation, it is ʿUmar.”

It is also reported that “truth was firmly established on his tongue and in his heart.” And he said:

“Had I not been sent among you, ʿUmar would have been sent among you.”

Despite this, he would not bind anyone to his own opinion or rule on public matters; rather, he would consult the Companions and reconsider. At times he would express a view, only to be corrected

translated_text:
by a woman, whose view he would then accept. For example, he wanted to set a limit on bridal gifts, so that they would not exceed those given to the Prophet’s wives—may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said, “Whoever gives more, the excess will be placed in the public treasury.” Muslims would pay the bridal gift before consummating the marriage; they deferred it only rarely.

A woman said, “Commander of the Faithful, why do you deny us something Allah has granted us in His Book?”

He asked, “Where?” She replied, “In His words, Most High:

‘If you wish to replace one wife with another, and have given one of them a great sum, do not take anything back from it.’”

So ʿUmar accepted her view and said, “A woman was right, and a man was wrong.”

In disputed matters, such as questions of inheritance and divorce, he would hold one view, ʿAlī ibn Abī Tālib another, ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd another, and Zayd ibn Thābit another. He did not compel anyone to adopt his position; rather, each of them would issue fatwas according to his own view, even though ʿUmar—may Allah be pleased with him—was the leader of the entire Muslim community, the most knowledgeable and devout among them, and the best of them. How, then, could any judge be better than ʿUmar?

This applies when he has ruled on a matter open to independent scholarly judgment. What, then, if his position has never been held by any of the imams of the Muslims—not the four imams, nor the Companions and Successors before them—but is held only by him and others like him who have no knowledge of the Book, the Sunnah, or the views of the early generations and the imams?

They merely judge according to the customs in which they were brought up, like those who said:

“We found our forefathers following a way, and we follow in their footsteps.”

translated_text:
the Bedouins according to their inherited precedents, which are customs, just as the Tatars judge according to the “Yāsiq,” which they customarily follow. As for people of faith, Islam, knowledge, and religious devotion, they judge only according to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, as Allah Most High says:

“But no, by your Lord, they will not believe until they make you judge in their disputes, then find within themselves no resistance to your judgment and submit completely.”

And Allah Most High says:

“Is it the judgment of the age of ignorance they seek? And who is better than Allah in judgment for people who are certain?”

Allah, glorified be He, did not deem the judgment of one person sufficient between spouses when discord is feared between them, since it is not known which of them is at fault and there is no evidence to establish this. Rather, He commanded the appointment of two arbitrators who must not be open to suspicion of bias: one from the husband’s family and one from the wife’s family. As Allah Most High says:

“If you fear a breach between them, appoint an arbitrator from his family and an arbitrator from hers. If they both desire reconciliation”—meaning the two arbitrators—“Allah will bring harmony between them”—meaning the spouses.

If the arbitrators consider it best to keep the spouses together, they do so; and if they consider it best to separate them, they do so. If the wife is at fault, the separation is in exchange for compensation she pays, making it a khulʿ divorce. If the husband is at fault, they are separated without his consent.

Most scholars hold that these two are arbitrators, as Allah has called them, and that they issue their judgment without being appointed as agents by the spouses. This is the position of Mālik, and one of the two views reported from each of al-Shāfiʿī and Imam Ahmad. Another view holds that they are agents, as maintained by Abū Hanīfah and in the other view within the two schools.

{فَفَهَّمْنَاهَا سُلَيْمَانَ وَكُلًّا آتَيْنَا حُكْمًا وَعِلْمًا}

" وَوَلِيُّ الْأَمْرِ "

translated_text:
Thus, in this case, when it was unclear who was in the right, Allah did not entrust judgment to one person, even though this concerned a particular dispute between two spouses. Even if a single judge were to rule between the spouses on a clear matter, his ruling would not be enforced, by agreement of the Muslims. How, then, could this be permitted in matters of religion and worship that concern all Muslims and have become unclear to many people?

By the consensus of the Muslims, judgment in such matters belongs to Allah and His Messenger alone. Whoever has knowledge of what the Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, brought should explain and clarify it to the Muslims. Once Muslims know the law of their Prophet, they will not depart from it. If, however, each group says, “We possess knowledge from the Messenger,” and there is no clear point on which they agree concerning their dispute, then one of the two groups receives two rewards and the other receives one reward. As Allah Most High says:

“And David and Solomon, when they judged concerning the field into which some people’s sheep had strayed by night; We were witness to their judgment.”

“We gave Solomon understanding of the case, and to each We gave wisdom and knowledge.”

As for “the ruler,” if he knows what the Book and the Sunnah teach, he must judge between people accordingly. If he does not know, but can learn what each side says until he recognizes the truth, he must judge according to it. If neither course is possible for him, he must leave the Muslims as they are, each worshipping Allah according to his own scholarly judgment. He has no right to compel anyone to accept another person’s opinion, even if he is a judge.

And when rulers depart from this, they judge by other than what Allah has revealed, and strife breaks out among them. The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“No people judge by other than what Allah has revealed without strife breaking out among them.”

This is among the greatest causes of changes in rule, as has happened time and again in our age and in earlier ages. Whoever Allah wills to grant happiness, He enables him to learn from what has befallen others, so that he follows the path of those whom Allah has supported and granted victory, and avoids the path of those whom Allah has forsaken and humiliated. For Allah says in His Book:

“Allah will surely support those who support Him. Indeed, Allah is Powerful and Almighty.”

“Those who, if We establish them in the land, establish prayer, give zakah, enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong. And to Allah belongs the outcome of all matters.”

Allah has thus promised to support those who support Him. Supporting Him means supporting His Book, His religion and His Messenger—not supporting those who judge by other than what Allah has revealed and speak without knowledge. For if a judge is devout but judges without knowledge, he is among the people of the Fire. If he is knowledgeable but judges contrary to the truth he knows, he is among the people of the Fire. If he judges with neither justice nor knowledge, he is all the more deserving of being among the people of the Fire. This applies when he judges a particular case concerning an individual.

But if he issues a general ruling concerning the Muslims’ religion, declaring truth to be falsehood and falsehood to be truth, the Sunnah to be innovation and innovation to be the Sunnah, right to be wrong and wrong to be right, forbidding what Allah and His Messenger have commanded and commanding what Allah and His Messenger have forbidden—then this is another matter entirely. Judgment in it belongs to the Lord of all worlds, the God of the messengers, the Master of the Day of Judgment, to whom

“belongs all praise in this world and the Hereafter. His is the judgment, and to Him you will be returned,”

“who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth to make it prevail over all religion. And sufficient is Allah as a Witness.”

All praise is due to Allah, Lord of all worlds. May Allah bless Muhammad, his family and his Companions, and grant them peace.

Shaykh al-Islām, may Allah have mercy on him, also said: (*)

The cases adjudicated by those in authority—whether they are called judges or governors, or whether some have at times been called wulāt al-ahdāth or officials charged with redressing grievances, or other customary, conventional titles—are all subject to the judgment of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, which encompasses all creation.

Everyone entrusted with the affairs of the Muslim community, or who adjudicates between two people, must judge with justice and equity, according to the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. This is the law revealed by Allah. Allah Most High says:

“We certainly sent Our messengers with clear proofs, and sent down with them the Scripture and the balance so that people may uphold justice. And We sent down iron, with its great might and benefits for people.”

He Most High also says:

“Indeed, Allah commands you to return trusts to their rightful owners and, when you judge between people, to judge with justice.”

He Most High also says:

“Indeed, We have sent down to you the Book in truth so that you may judge between people by what Allah has shown you.”

He Most High also says:

“So judge between them by what Allah has revealed, and do not follow their desires.”

Cases fall into two categories: those involving an accusation and those that do not. A case involving an accusation is one in which the claimant alleges that the defendant committed an act forbidden to him that warrants punishment, such as killing or highway robbery

(*) Shaykh Nāsir ibn Hamad al-Fahd said (pp. 247–249):
Several points should be noted here:

First: Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, included this fatwa in his book al-Turuq al-Hukmiyya, pp. 93–108.

Second: These remarks by Shaykh al-Islām, may Allah have mercy on him, answered a question omitted from al-Fatāwā but included in al-Turuq al-Hukmiyya, p. 93, where Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, said:
“I have seen a question and answer on this matter by Shaykh al-Islām Ibn Taymiyya, may Allah have mercy on him and be pleased with him:
‘Do measures of governance involving the beating and imprisonment of accused persons in lawsuits and other matters form part of revealed law? If so, who deserves such treatment, and who does not? What should be the extent of the beating and the duration of imprisonment?’
He answered: ‘The cases adjudicated by those in authority, whether they are called judges or governors…’”

Third: Comparison reveals some omissions and textual corruptions. Among the most important are:

1 – 35/391: “Ibn ‘Abbās [is the one who narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that ‘he assigned the oath to the defendant’; he is also] the one who narrates from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that he adjudicated on the basis of an oath together with a witness.” The words in square brackets are missing from al-Fatāwā but appear in al-Turuq, p. 95.

2 – 35/395: “And sometimes a man and two women.” This is an error; the correct reading is: “And sometimes it is a man and two women,” as in al-Turuq, p. 96.

3 – 35/400: “They supposed that revealed law alone could not [sustain] the governance of the world.” The word in square brackets is missing from al-Fatāwā but appears in al-Turuq, p. 104.

4 – 35/405: The Shaykh, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned three opinions concerning the extent of ta‘zīr (discretionary punishment), beginning with:
“The first, and best, is the view of a group of the followers of al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad, and others: for each offense, discretionary punishment must fall short of the prescribed punishment for that offense, even if it exceeds a punishment prescribed for another offense…”

In al-Turuq, p. 107, Ibn al-Qayyim, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned four opinions. The first—the fourth view, which is absent from al-Fatāwā—is:
“It is determined by the public interest and is proportionate to the offense; the ruler exercises his judgment in determining it.”

The point is that, after mentioning these opinions, he said in both al-Fatāwā and al-Turuq:
“According to the first opinion, may such punishment extend to execution, as in the execution of a Muslim spy…?”

In al-Fatāwā, this refers to the position that “for each offense, discretionary punishment must fall short of the prescribed punishment for that offense.”

In al-Turuq, it refers to the position that “it is determined by the public interest.”

The more likely conclusion is that the text in al-Turuq al-Hukmiyya is correct and that an omission has occurred in al-Fatāwā—and Allah knows best. His words, “According to the first opinion, may such punishment extend to execution?” indicate that the discretionary punishment in question is not subject to a specified limit. By contrast, the first opinion mentioned in al-Fatāwā stipulates that, for each offense, discretionary punishment must fall short of its prescribed punishment. This question therefore does not arise under that position; it arises only under the position that makes the punishment dependent on the public interest. Allah Most High knows best.

translated_text:
or theft, or other forms of unlawful aggression, such as acts committed secretly in ways that ordinarily make it impossible, in most cases, to establish proof of them. A case not involving an accusation is a claim concerning a contract—such as a sale, loan, pledge, or guarantee—or a claim that does not arise from an unlawful act, such as an established debt arising from a purchase price, loan, bridal due, compensation for harm caused unintentionally, or the like.

Either category may involve a claim concerning a prescribed punishment that is exclusively a right of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as with drinking intoxicants and unlawful sexual intercourse. It may concern an exclusively human right, as with financial claims, or it may involve both, as with theft and highway robbery. In these two “categories,” unless the claimant presents proof recognized by Islamic law, the defendant’s statement is accepted upon his taking an oath. This is based on what Muslim narrated in his Sahīh from Ibn ‘Abbās, who said that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“If people were granted what they claimed merely on the basis of their claims, some would lay claim to other men’s lives and property. Rather, the oath is incumbent upon the defendant.”

Another narration from Ibn ‘Abbās in the two Sahīh collections states:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled that the oath was incumbent upon the defendant.”

This hadith explicitly states that no one is to be granted anything merely on the basis of his claim. It also explicitly states that, in a claim seeking an award, the defendant is initially required to take an oath. It does not state that claims warranting punishment require nothing more than an oath from the defendant. Rather, it is established that he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: “

to the Ansār when they complained to him about their slain kinsman, ‘Abdullāh ibn Sahl, who had been killed at Khaybar. His brother ‘Abd al-Rahmān and his paternal cousins Huwayyisa and Muhayyisa came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. Muhayyisa had been with him at Khaybar. He said:

‘Will you swear fifty oaths and thereby establish your right over your kinsman’s killer?’

They replied, ‘How can we swear when we neither witnessed nor saw what happened?’

He said, ‘Then the Jews can clear themselves of your accusation by swearing fifty oaths.’

They replied, ‘How can we accept the oaths of people who are unbelievers?’”

This was reported by all the compilers of the Sahīh and Sunan collections, including al-Bukhārī, Muslim, Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, and al-Nasā’ī. In one narration in the two Sahīh collections, he said:

“Fifty of you shall swear oaths against a man from among them, and he will be handed over to you, bound.”

It is also established in Sahīh Muslim, on the authority of Ibn ‘Abbās, that:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, ruled on the basis of one witness and an oath.”

Al-Tirmidhī and Ibn Mājah reported this from Jābir, while Abū Dāwūd, al-Tirmidhī, and Ibn Mājah reported it from Abū Hurayrah. It has also been narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, through many other routes. These hadiths are the most authentic and widely known reports narrated from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, on this subject. Ibn ‘Abbās himself narrates from the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, that “he ruled on the basis of an oath together with a witness”; the Prophet gave one ruling in some claims and the other ruling in others.

As for the hadith commonly quoted by jurists:

“Proof is incumbent upon the claimant, and an oath upon the one who denies the claim,”

this too has been narrated. However, its chain of transmission does not match the others in authenticity and renown, nor was it reported by most compilers of the well-known Sunan collections.  وَأَجَابُوا عَنْ ذَلِكَ الْحَدِيثِ:
 تَارَةً بِالتَّضْعِيفِ. وَتَارَةً بِأَنَّهُ عَامٌّ وَأَحَادِيثُهُمْ خَاصَّةٌ. وَتَارَةً بِأَنَّ أَحَادِيثَهُمْ أَصَحُّ وَأَكْثَرُ وَأَشْهَرُ؛ فَالْعَمَلُ بِهَا عِنْدَ التَّعَارُضِ أَوْلَى وَقَدْ ثَبَتَ عَنْ النَّبِيِّ صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ أَنَّهُ طَلَبَ الْبَيِّنَةَ مِنْ الْمُدَّعِي وَالْيَمِينَ مِنْ الْمُنْكِرِ فِي حُكُومَاتٍ مُعَيَّنَةٍ؛ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ جِنْسِ دَعَاوَى التُّهَمِ؛
translated_text:
hold that the oath must always be taken by the party denying the claim. Even in the oath procedure for homicide cases, they require the defendant to swear; they do not rule on the basis of one witness and an oath, nor do they refer the oath back to the claimant when the defendant refuses to swear. They cite the general wording of this hadith as evidence.

As for the other scholars of the Muslim community—from Medina, Mecca, and Syria, as well as the jurists versed in hadith and others, such as Ibn Jurayh, Mālik, al-Layth ibn Sa‘d, al-Shāfi‘ī, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ishāq ibn Rāhawayh, and others—they sometimes require the claimant to swear and sometimes the defendant, in accordance with the established practices of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The principle held by most of them is that the oath is prescribed for the party whose case is stronger.

In their usage, “proof” denotes whatever makes the truth clear. They differ over the detailed applications of this principle: proof may consist of circumstantial evidence together with the oaths prescribed in homicide cases; it may consist of one witness and an oath; or it may consist of evidence other than witnesses, such as a description identifying lost property.

They have answered that hadith in several ways: by judging it weak; by arguing that its wording is general, whereas the hadiths they cite concern specific cases; or by maintaining that their hadiths are more authentic, more numerous, and better known, and thus deserve precedence when the reports conflict. It is established that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, required proof from the claimant and an oath from the party denying the claim in certain disputes that did not involve claims based on suspicion;

translated_text:
such as the report recorded in the two authentic hadith collections from al-Ash‘ath ibn Qays, who said:

“I had a dispute with a man over a well, and we brought our case before the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He said: ‘Produce your two witnesses; otherwise, he must swear an oath.’ I said: ‘Then he will swear without a care!’ He replied: ‘Whoever swears a false oath to deprive a Muslim of his property will meet Allah while He is angry with him.’”

In another version, he said: “Produce your evidence that the well is yours; otherwise, he must swear an oath.”

It is also narrated from Wā’il ibn Hujr, who said:

“A man from Hadramawt and a man from Kindah came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. The man from Hadramawt said: ‘O Messenger of Allah, this man has seized land that belonged to my father.’ The man from Kindah said: ‘It is my land, in my possession, and I cultivate it. He has no right to it.’

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, asked the man from Hadramawt: ‘Do you have any proof?’ He replied: ‘No.’ He said: ‘Then you are entitled to require his oath.’ The man said: ‘O Messenger of Allah, he is wicked. He does not care what he swears to and has no scruples about anything.’ He replied: ‘You are entitled to nothing more from him.’

“When the man turned away, the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: ‘If he swears an oath concerning property in order to appropriate it wrongfully, he will surely meet Allah while He turns away from him.’”

Reported by Muslim and al-Tirmidhī, who graded it authentic.

This authentic hadith shows that he required nothing of the defendant beyond an oath, even though the claimant had mentioned his wickedness. He said: “You are entitled to nothing more from him.” Likewise, in the first hadith, al-Ash‘ath’s opponent was a Jew, as stated in the two authentic collections. Nevertheless, he required nothing of him beyond an oath. And in the hadith concerning the oath procedure in homicide cases, when the Ansār said:

translated_text:
“How can we accept the oaths of unbelievers?” he did not object to their saying this. Thus, it is clear that claims differ in this respect. I know of no disagreement concerning this category: namely, that the defendant’s word is accepted under oath if the claimant produces no legally valid proof—that is, evidence.

Evidence constituting legally valid proof may consist of two upright male witnesses, or one man and two women. It may consist of four witnesses, or, according to some scholars among the followers of Ahmad and some followers of al-Shāfi‘ī, three witnesses. The latter concerns a claim of insolvency by someone known to have possessed wealth. For it is reported in Sahīh Muslim, from Qabīsah ibn Mukhāriq al-Hilālī, that the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said:

“Begging is lawful only for three kinds of men: a man who has assumed a financial liability, for whom begging is lawful until he obtains enough to discharge it, after which he must refrain; a man whose property has been swept away by a calamity, for whom begging is lawful until he obtains enough to sustain himself; and a man afflicted by poverty—once three men of sound judgment from his people come forward and say, ‘So-and-so has indeed been afflicted by poverty,’ begging becomes lawful for him until he obtains enough to sustain himself. Any begging beyond these cases, O Qabīsah, is unlawful gain, which its recipient consumes unlawfully.”

Another reason is that wealth is a hidden matter, giving rise to a strong suspicion that assets are being concealed.

At times, proof consists of one witness together with the claimant’s oath, according to the majority of Muslim jurists among the scholars of the Hijāz and the jurists of hadith.

At times, proof consists of women’s testimony: either one woman, according to Abū Hanīfah and the best-known view reported from Ahmad; two women, according to Mālik and one view reported from Ahmad; or four women, according to al-Shāfi‘ī. At other times, proof takes some other form.

translated_text:
At other times, proof consists of circumstantial indications, incriminating circumstances, and suspicion, together with fifty oaths sworn by the claimant. This is the procedure known as qasāmah, in which the claimant’s oaths are taken first according to most jurists of the Hijāz and scholars of hadith. It differs from other procedures in requiring fifty oaths, just as the oaths of mutual imprecation are distinguished by consisting of four testimonies sworn by Allah, since each oath takes the place of a witness. According to Mālik and Ahmad, qasāmah establishes liability to retaliatory execution, whereas according to al-Shāfi‘ī it establishes liability only to blood money. The jurists of opinion administer the oaths only to the defendant, as mentioned earlier, yet they still require him to pay blood money despite his having sworn them. There are well-known details concerning this, which are not our purpose to discuss here.

Our purpose is simply to draw attention to the principal rulings governing legal claims, for this is a subject of great importance, and the need for it is both pressing and widespread. Neglect by some authorities and transgression by others have led to ignorance of the truth and injustice towards people. The term “religious law” has consequently ceased to correspond to its original meaning. Rather, in these times it is used in three senses.

The first is revealed law: the Quran and the Sunnah. Following it is obligatory, and whoever departs from it must be put to death. It encompasses the fundamentals of religion and its subsidiary rulings, the administration of rulers and those entrusted with public funds, the judgments of judges, the leadership exercised by shaykhs, and other matters. No one, whether among earlier or later generations, may depart from obedience to Allah and His Messenger.

The second is the law as interpreted: matters over which the Muslim community differs and exercises independent juristic reasoning. Whoever adopts a position in a matter legitimately open to such reasoning is allowed to maintain it; others are not all required to agree with him except on the basis of incontrovertible proof from the Quran and the Sunnah.

And the third is altered law: what is established through false testimony, judgments rendered in ignorance and injustice rather than justice and truth—thus judging by other than what Allah has revealed—or instructions to make a false acknowledgment that deprives someone of a right. An example is instructing a sick person to make an unfounded acknowledgment in favour of one heir, thereby invalidating the rights of the remaining heirs. Giving such instructions and bearing witness to such an acknowledgment are forbidden. However, a judge who is unaware of the true circumstances incurs no sin if he rules according to what appears to him to be right. The foremost of judges, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said in the hadith recorded by both al-Bukhārī and Muslim:

“You bring your disputes before me, and some of you may present their case more eloquently than others. I judge only according to what I hear. If I award anyone something that rightfully belongs to his brother, he must not take it, for I am only allotting him a piece of the Fire.”

The other category of legal claims consists of “claims involving criminal accusations”: allegations of crimes and forbidden acts, such as killing, highway robbery, theft, and aggression against others through beating or other means. In such cases, defendants fall into three categories. The accused may be someone who is not the sort of person to commit the alleged offence; a wicked person of that sort; or someone whose character is unknown to the judge. If he is upright, there is agreement that he may not be punished.

Mālik’s followers and others said: “The rightful owner swears that it is his property and has not passed out of his ownership, and then takes it back.” They hold that the defendant is not required to swear an oath. They then differed over whether the accuser should be punished.

Mālik and Ashhab said: “The claimant is not to be disciplined unless he intended to harm, discredit and insult the defendant, in which case he is to be disciplined.”

Asbagh said: “He is to be disciplined whether or not he intended to harm him.” Likewise, scholars generally hold that defendants are not required to swear oaths concerning the prescribed punishments that are Allah’s rights. Once the rightful owner has recovered his property, no claim remains against those possessing it except one concerning the prescribed punishment, and no oath is required.

The second category

The accused may be someone whose character is unknown, who is known neither for righteousness nor for wickedness. According to the generality of Muslim scholars, such a person is detained until his circumstances become clear. The explicit position of most leading scholars is that both the judge and the governor may detain him. This was expressly stated by Mālik and his followers; it is also the explicit position of Imam Ahmad and the most discerning scholars among his followers, and was mentioned by the followers of Abū Hanīfah.

Imam Ahmad said: “The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, detained someone on suspicion.” Ahmad said: “That is until his circumstances become clear to the judge.” This is based on the report narrated by Abū Dāwūd in his Sunan, al-Khallāl and others, from Bahz ibn Hakīm, from his father, from his grandfather:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, detained someone on suspicion.”

Al-Khallāl also narrated from Abū Hurayrah:

“The Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, detained someone on suspicion for a day and a night.”

The defendant thus remains detained and restrained from the time he is summoned until the dispute between him and his opponent is settled. This is detention without suspicion; detention on suspicion is therefore all the more warranted.

“Detention under Islamic law” does not mean confinement in a cramped place. Rather, it means restraining a person and preventing him from moving about freely, whether in a house or a mosque, or by placing him in the custody of his opponent or his opponent’s representative. This is why the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, called such a person a captive. Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah narrated from al-Hirmās ibn Habīb, from his father, who said:

“I brought a debtor of mine to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. He told me, ‘Stay with him.’ Then he said, ‘O brother of Banū Tamīm, what do you intend to do with your captive?’”

the scholars among Ahmad’s followers and others differed over whether the ruler should establish a prison, holding two views. Those who held that he should not establish a prison said that he should restrain the person in some location or appoint a guard over him—a practice known as “guarded custody.”

Accordingly, since attendance at the judge’s court entails restraint and restriction akin to imprisonment and detention, the scholars differed: should the defendant be summoned merely on the basis of a claim? Or, if appearing would demean him, should he not be summoned until some basis for the claimant’s case becomes apparent? There are two views, both reported from Ahmad. The second is Mālik’s view, while the first is that of Abū Hanīfah and al-Shāfi‘ī.

Some scholars held that detention on suspicion falls within the authority of the governor responsible for military affairs, not the judge. This view was mentioned by a number of al-Shāfi‘ī’s followers, such as Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Zubayrī, Chief Judge al-Māwardī and others, as well as by some of Ahmad’s followers who wrote on judicial conduct, and others.

They also differed over the duration of detention on suspicion: is it fixed, or is it left to the ruler’s judgment? These are two views mentioned by Judge Abū Ya‘lā, Judge al-Māwardī and others. It was said that it is fixed at one month; this is the view of Abū ‘Abd Allāh al-Zubayrī. It was also said that it has no fixed duration; this is the view preferred by al-Māwardī.

translated_text:
The third category is where the accused is known for wrongdoing: for example, someone accused of theft who was previously known for it, someone accused of highway robbery who was known for it, or someone accused of murder; or where any of these persons is known for conduct that gives grounds for such an accusation. If detaining someone whose character is unknown is permissible, then detaining someone known for wrongdoing is all the more justified.

I know of none of the authoritative imams of the Muslims who held that, in all such cases, the defendant should swear an oath and then be released by any of the authorities, without detention or any other measure. No imam holds this position without qualification. Whoever claims that this, in its unrestricted and universal application, is the religious law has committed a gross error, contrary to the explicit teachings of Allah’s Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the consensus of the Muslim community.

Such gross errors have emboldened rulers to contravene the religious law. They imagined that the religious law alone could not provide for the governance of society and the interests of the Muslim community, and consequently transgressed Allah’s limits in these matters. Both groups’ ignorance of the true nature of the religious law has led people to abandon it in favour of various innovations in governance.

This category includes cases involving qasāmah—the procedure of fifty oaths in homicide cases. Its rulings are well known and need not be mentioned here. As for accusations of theft, highway robbery and similar offences, detention in such cases has already been discussed.

As for questioning through beating and similar means, scholars differed: is it authorized for both the judge and the governor? Or for the governor but not the judge? Or is beating authorized for either of them? There are three views.
